Tariffs are a double-edged sword whose effects on the economy are much more complex than simply “oh, this way the local product will cost less, so people will buy local”. The price distortion introduced by tariffs is only local, meaning that it doesn't have a benefit for export, and can in fact become counterproductive in case of tariff wars (nation A puts tariffs on product P to avoid importing that much, so nation B puts tariffs on product D which was a significant part of A's export). It can also lead to the price of the local to increase, which again can be detrimental for the internal market.

For example, the last time steel tariffs were added (2002, under Bush) they had to be lifted after one year because they had actually been found to be counter-productive: they damaged the rest of the industry more than they benefited specifically the steel production.

And that was just in the short term. In the longer term, lack of competition can lead to the industry “settling down” and stopping being innovative due to lack of competition. There's no reason to make the process more efficient, or the product itself better, if people are going to buy yours anyway because foreign products, albeit better and produced more efficiently, are too expensive.

Whether or not this happens is extremely dependent on the context, on the tariff and a number of other factors. A positive example was the US steel market in the XIX century, which massively reinvested the high profits due to the overpricing of the local product allowed by the tariffs and resulted in significant improvements to the manufacturing process. A negative example is Brazil today, where the high tariffs are only used as an excuse to jack up the price, with no meaningful growth in competitiveness.

Ultimately, the medium and long term effect of tariffs isn't easy to prove positive, without the proper oversight.

Again, it's not that simple.

First of all, the manufacturing industry hardly “evaporated”; in fact its output not only never decreased (except during the recession in 2008–2010), it grew despite the reduction in workforce; the only reason why it's “only” the second-largest in the world is that the first one is China, but then again, we're talking about over 1 billion people versus less than a third of that.

When talking about employment, it's true that a decade after the lowering of tariffs, at the turn of the century, manufacturing experienced a significant drop in employment. And while China's competition is definitely one factor that could have been amortized by higher tariffs, it's hardly the only one. There was also a significant shift of investments from manufacturing to the financial sector (arguably one of the main reasons for the 2008 recession) and other “virtual” productivity (remember the dot-com bubble?), as well as nontrivial changes to the US monetary policy, all combined with improvements to manufacturing and distribution processes.

The next drop in employment, which was much worse than the previous (nearly 3M job lost in two years) happened nearly a decade later, and was mostly due to the recession. Tariffs would have hardly helped (just like the Smoot-Hawley tariffs did nothing to spare the US from the Great Depression —and if anything contributed to precipitating it). And of course, since 2010, the manufacturing industry in the US has grown also in employment (recovering ~1M units, more or less the same amount that were lost in 2001), despite the lack of tariffs.

And that's just manufacturing; a more interesting analysis would be the impact of (lack of) tariffs on the overall economy, especially since with technological progress the contraction of employment in manufacturing is essentially inevitable anyway (in fact, the US growth in output despite the decrease in employment is an outstanding marker of this).
